newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution rests in Garcia Abrego trial.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution rests in Garcia Abrego trial.

text.p: Prosecutors on Monday wrapped up their case against Juan Garcia Abrego with testimony from a U.S. agent who said the reputed drug kingpin admitted smuggling marijuana and cocaine into the United States.

Drug Enforcement Administration agent Joe Dubois, the U.S. government's final witness after three weeks of testimony, said Garcia Abrego told investigators after his Jan. 14 capture that he shipped up to 1,000 pounds (450 kg) of marijuana and 220 pounds (100 kg) of cocaine a month from his base in northern Mexico, but denied he was a major trafficker.

"He said he never moved the large amounts (of drugs that he was reputed to have moved)," Dubois said in recounting Garcia Abrego's hourlong interrogation at FBI offices in Houston, where he was flown two days after his arrest in Monterrey, Mexico.

Garcia Abrego, once on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list, faces life in prison if convicted on 22 drug-related counts. The government said he led the Gulf Cartel, which at one time shipped up to a third of the cocaine used in the United States.
He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
Dubois said Garcia Abrego told agents he got his cocaine from Colombia and would smuggle it across the Rio Grande in exchange for a share of the load.

The smuggling was made easy by an arrangement with Mexican federal police commanders along the border who would call all their officers into headquarters when the cartel needed to make a shipment, Garcia Abrego said.
Garcia Abrego also admitted to paying a bribe to FBI agent Claudio de la O, who attempted to infiltrate the cartel by posing as a corrupt officer, Dubois said.
The accused drug dealer implied during the interview that he would make a deal with investigators in exchange for information about another trafficker, Dubois said.
"It (the offer of a deal) was so self-serving that we all had to laugh about it ... even he laughed," Dubois told the eight-man, four-woman jury in U.S. District Judge Ewing Werlein's court.
Defence attorneys, who have argued that prosecutors have the wrong man, began putting on what they said would be a handful of witnesses to try to discredit Garcia Abrego's post-capture statement.

They said he was too high on Valium pumped into him by Mexican officials before his flight to Houston to know what he was saying. Dubois testified that Garcia Abrego appeared to be in control of his thoughts and not intoxicated.
The case was expected to go to the jury later this week after closing arguments by the opposing lawyers.
